Big Country - In A Big Country

Vinny began his playthrough last night and... well, the game is better than I remember it. The lush setting, the mechanics. Enough people know about these things already that I'm not going to repeat them.

The springtime of youth

What's more interesting to me, after seeing a bit of this game again today, is to think about the story in the context of when it was made: the mid-90s. The playstation era always seemed to me like the SNES era's pubescent older brother. If you had a SNES when you were 10, you'd likely be around 15 when the PS1 came out. The demographic was growing up, so the games followed suit.

Just to paint a picture for you, Chrono Trigger never thought much about sex or relationships: Marle and Lucca are introduced to us in short order, and it would only be conventional that they both be love interests, but Lucca seems more interested in teledildonics than in Crono. Ayla is somewhat suggestive in her introduction when you first meet her, but we're informed that she's fated to be with Kino... even though he's kind of a loser. Poor Ayla. The point being, Crono and Marle's pairing is the only one seriously entertained by the plot, and even that is mostly implied by Marle's immediate, intense liking for Crono, and a few scenes throughout the game all of which have a completely innocent interpretation. The tension is minimal, and there's no love triangle.

Chrono Cross seems to do things differently. Leena (the stand-in for Lucca, the girl-next-door) talks about marriage, and their inexorable transition into adulthood. I remembered the feeling I got reading those lines for the first time. Fear and anticipation. That seems to speak more powerfully than most of CT, especially to its target audience who were themselves on the cusp of adulthood.

My expectation going forward is that where CT was more sci-fi oriented— it cared more about its main conflict and about having a fun time sci-fi adventure— CC will be somewhat more serious and more character-driven. (Until the final third, where the plot devolves into nonsense about a giant robot baby or something. I really can't remember.)

The cogs of fate

There are, of course, no literal cogs of fate, but the opening cutscene makes this allusion. Their "movement" is, I think, a metaphor for the exercise of one's faculty of choice. When you reach beyond instinct and routine, you feel something altered your own fate.

Both CT and CC are good about driving that point home: your actions make a difference. We've already met that one fisherman whose other-world self didn't follow his dream. It'll be interesting to see how this theme develops.

The plot is on easy-mode

Something that surprised me is how readily "Another Leena" joins the party. After the awkward first meeting, I expected that she would remain distant and mistrustful, and that it would be Home Leena that joins. That'd give it more of a dramatic edge: you have this one person who wants to be your #1 waifu, and the other who thinks you're probably a child molester because her first impression of you was you babbling at her like a crazy person.

It would've made more sense (and technically correct is the best kind of correct, right?) but what we really want is to add depth to the cast. Vinny's already talked about how there are a few dozen characters, and they're all fairly shallow, so having characters make absurd decisions doesn't tend to ameliorate that.

And to be fair, CT wasn't great with character development, either. After the halfway point, the characters are mostly one-note. Ayla, for example, has nothing to say for the rest of the game except that she wants to punch and/or eat things. That's of necessity, as it is in CC, because the characters are literally interchangeable, so there isn't room for each character to develop in events that don't involve them specifically.

This is a lot of words

I hope someone else reads this and decides to join me in revisiting Chrono Cross and thinking way too hard about videogames.
